series.name: Before The Signboard
series.tagline: What happened before the business had a name people recognized.
series.concept: An unnamed interviewer travels across India — cities, towns, villages — meeting people who built businesses from scratch. Each episode is one place, one founder, one story. The focus is on the hardships, the near-failures, the ugly early days. Not all businesses succeed. Core thesis: Choose the struggle you want to endure, not the outcome you want to get. Money is a byproduct.

episodes.title: The Teacher Who Wouldn't Stop

slides.text: The Teacher Who Wouldn't Stop

Kota smells like chalk dust and desperation.

Every second building is a coaching center. Every third face is a 17-year-old carrying the weight of a family's future.

I'm here to meet a man who looked at all of this and thought: "I should open one more."

Ramesh Yadav was a government school teacher. Stable salary. Pension. The kind of job people in his family prayed for.

He quit.

Not because he hated teaching. Because the system wouldn't let him teach the way he wanted to.

He rented two rooms above a chai shop. Bought a whiteboard. Printed 500 pamphlets.

Month 1: Zero students.
Month 2: Zero students.
Month 3: The landlord came.

"Agla mahina rent nahi aaya toh taala lagega."

His first batch: 11 students.

Most were kids whose parents couldn't afford Allen. Ramesh was the budget option. The last resort.

Four dropped out within two months.

Seven remained. He taught them like his life depended on it. Because it did.

One student cracked NEET.

One. Out of seven.

Her name was Priya Meena. Her photo went up on the wall. Parents started calling.

But don't mistake this for a turning point.

It took Ramesh three more years to break even. Three years of 14-hour days and a wife who packed tiffin for 30 students because they couldn't afford a canteen.

Today, Ramesh has 400 students. A proper building. AC classrooms.

But he still teaches the first batch himself. Every year. The weakest students. The ones nobody else wants.

"Allen aur Bansal se compete nahi karna tha. Unke reject mujhe chahiye the."

Ramesh didn't choose coaching for the money.

He chose it because he couldn't stop teaching.

The struggle of watching students fail and trying harder — that was a struggle he could endure.

Not everyone can stand in an empty room for three months. He could. Because the room wasn't the point. The whiteboard was.

I travel across India — cities, towns, villages.

I meet people who built something from nothing. Not all of them succeeded. Most nearly didn't.

This isn't a success story series. It's about what happened before the business had a name.

The ugly early days. The near-failures. The struggles people chose.

25 episodes. 25 cities. 25 stories.

This is Before The Signboard.

Follow @the.unwritten.rules

episodes.synopsis: In Kota, a city that runs on coaching, a government teacher quits his secure job to open his own institute. Three months pass with zero students. His landlord wants him out, his in-laws mock him, and his first batch of 11 students starts shrinking. One NEET result changes everything — but breaking even takes three more years.
episodes.caption: Kota has 100+ coaching centers. He opened one more. Know someone who started something in a city that already had too much of it?

episodes.title: The Diamond That Didn't Shine

slides.text: The Diamond That Didn't Shine

Surat doesn't look like a diamond city from the outside.

It looks like every other Gujarati trading town — narrow streets, dabbas, men in white shirts doing deals on phone.

But behind the shutters, in windowless rooms, hundreds of hands are cutting and polishing stones worth more than the buildings they sit in.

Mehul's family had been trading diamonds for three generations. Buy rough. Sell polished. The margins were thin but steady.

Mehul had an MBA and a spreadsheet.

"If we polish in-house, we keep 30% more margin."

His father said no. Mehul went ahead anyway.

He hired 40 artisans. Rented a floor. Bought polishing equipment.

Within three months, the bigger units came hunting.

They offered his best workers 20% more. Then 30%.

Mehul couldn't match it. He was paying rent on a new floor with zero track record.

Eight workers left in the first quarter. The best eight.

Quality dropped. Fast.

The new hires were inexperienced. Cuts were uneven. Two shipments got rejected.

Clients who'd bought from his father for decades started calling.

Not to complain. To cancel.

14 months. That's how long it lasted.

Mehul shut the polishing unit. Returned the equipment at a loss. Let the remaining workers go.

The family's trading business took two more years to recover. Some clients never came back.

His father still hasn't said "I told you so." That's worse.

Mehul chose the outcome: vertical integration. Higher margins. A bigger name.

He didn't choose the struggle.

Managing 40 artisans. Retaining talent against bigger players. Maintaining quality on a factory floor.

He had no appetite for any of it.

The spreadsheet said 30% more margin. It didn't mention the 14-hour days on a polishing floor or the workers who'd leave for Rs. 2,000 more.

Next stop: Mumbai.

A woman in Dadar whose husband's business failed.

She started packing tiffins from her kitchen. 15 at first.

Now it's 500.

But the food poisoning scare in year two almost ended everything.

episodes.synopsis: In Surat, a young man from a diamond trading family tries to vertically integrate by opening a polishing unit. Skilled workers get poached, quality drops, clients leave, and the family name takes a hit. He shuts down in 14 months. The trading business suffers too.
episodes.caption: Ever seen someone chase the margin and miss the grind? Surat has a thousand stories like this.

episodes.title: The Tiffin That Fed Dadar

slides.text: The Tiffin That Fed Dadar

Dadar at 6 AM is already running.

Flower market. Fish market. Locals packed so tight you can't breathe.

I climb three floors to a flat where the entire hallway smells of dal tadka and roti.

Sunita opens the door in a kitchen apron. She's already been cooking for two hours.

Sunita's husband Manoj had a garment trading business. Small but enough.

Then demonetization happened. Then GST. Then a client defaulted on Rs. 8 lakh.

The business didn't collapse dramatically. It just stopped working. Like a fan that slows down and then stops.

Two kids. One income. Gone.

Sunita started with 15 tiffins.

Neighbours. Office workers in the building. A friend's friend.

Rs. 80 per tiffin. Two sabzi, dal, rice, roti.

She cooked on a two-burner stove. Packed in steel dabbas. Delivered them herself on the local train.

15 tiffins. Rs. 1,200 a day. Just enough to not borrow.

Scaling from 15 to 200 nearly killed it.

She couldn't cook alone. Hired a helper — he didn't show up half the time. Delivery boys quit because the pay was less than Swiggy.

Then the food poisoning scare.

Three customers sick on the same day. Word spread fast. 40 cancellations in a week.

Sunita didn't sleep for three days. Cleaned everything. Changed her oil supplier. Called every single customer personally.

The other struggle nobody talks about: her husband.

Manoj couldn't handle it. His wife earning. His wife getting calls. His wife being the reason the family ate.

"Log kya kahenge" wasn't just a phrase. It was a daily fight.

Sunita didn't have time for the fight. She had 200 tiffins to pack by 10 AM.

The turning point wasn't a viral moment. It was a system.

Sunita hired two women from her building. Same situation — husbands' incomes weren't enough.

They split the cooking. Standardized the menu. Bought bigger vessels.

Today: 500 tiffins across Dadar and Parel. 12 women. 6 delivery boys. One WhatsApp number that never stops buzzing.

Sunita didn't plan a business.

She planned to feed her kids.

The struggle of waking at 4 AM, cooking for strangers, managing a kitchen — she'd been doing it her whole life.

She just started getting paid for it.

That's the thing about choosing the right struggle. Sometimes you don't even realize you already have.

Next stop: Coimbatore.

An engineering graduate who said no to an IT job in Chennai.

He wanted to make auto parts with his hands. His first machine broke in two months.

His father mortgaged the family's farmland to keep him going.

episodes.synopsis: In Mumbai, a woman starts delivering home-cooked tiffins from her Dadar kitchen after her husband's business fails. She scales from 15 to 500 tiffins, surviving a food poisoning scare, unreliable delivery boys, and a husband who can't accept his wife is the breadwinner.
episodes.caption: 500 tiffins a day. Started with a two-burner stove. What's the most incredible small business in your neighborhood?

episodes.title: Grease Over Code

slides.text: Grease Over Code

Coimbatore smells like machine oil and ambition.

The auto parts belt is a maze of small workshops — tin roofs, CNC machines humming, men with grease-stained hands making components to micron-level precision.

I find Karthik's workshop on an industrial estate. It's clean. Unnervingly clean for a machine shop.

Karthik had an IT offer from a Chennai company. Rs. 6.5 lakh per annum. AC office. Stock options in three years.

He turned it down.

His mother cried. His classmates thought he was insane.

"Enna da, engineering padichitu workshop la velai pannuva?"

He didn't want to write code. He wanted to make things he could hold.

He bought a second-hand lathe machine on loan. Rs. 4 lakh. No warranty — because second-hand.

Two months in, the spindle failed.

Repair cost: Rs. 1.2 lakh. He didn't have it.

His father mortgaged two acres of farmland in their village. Land that had been in the family for three generations.

Karthik's hands shook when he signed the papers.

First big order: 10,000 brake disc components for a Tier-2 auto supplier.

Karthik delivered them on time. Proud. Relieved.

Quality check: rejected.

Tolerance was off by 0.05mm on 60% of the batch. In auto parts, that's not close enough. That's scrap.

He had to redo all 10,000 pieces. At his own cost. It nearly wiped him out.

He redid every piece. Checked every single one himself.

Then he did something nobody expected.

He documented everything. Process sheets. Quality logs. Rejection analysis. Cleanliness protocols.

A Tier-1 auto supplier visited for a routine audit. They expected a typical small workshop.

They found documentation better than factories ten times the size.

They gave him a trial order. That one contract changed everything.

Today, Karthik supplies to three Tier-1 companies. 22 employees. The farmland is back in his father's name.

But every new batch still gets the same treatment. Every part measured. Every log filled.

The 10,000 rejected pieces sit in a box in his office.

"Woh box hata nahi raha. Reminder hai."

Everyone told Karthik IT was the safe bet.

He chose grease over code because he loved making things you could hold.

The 10,000 rejected pieces didn't break him. They made his quality obsession permanent.

He didn't endure the struggle because he had to.

He endured it because making a perfect part — feeling it, measuring it, knowing it would go into a machine that works — that was worth every failed batch.

Next stop: Jaipur.

A couple who fell in love with a crumbling haveli.

They saw a boutique heritage homestay. Instagram-worthy. Five-star reviews.

What they got was plumbing permits, heritage regulations, and a renovation bill that tripled.

Not all stories end well.

episodes.synopsis: In Coimbatore, an engineering graduate turns down an IT job in Chennai to start a small auto parts workshop. His first machine breaks down, his father mortgages farmland, and his first big order gets rejected on quality. A Tier-1 supplier's trial order changes everything — but only because 10,000 rejected pieces made his quality obsession permanent.
episodes.caption: IT job or workshop floor? What did you turn down to do what you actually wanted? Or did you take the safe bet?

episodes.title: The Haveli That Looked Better Online

slides.text: The Haveli That Looked Better Online

Jaipur's old city is a maze of narrow lanes and faded grandeur.

Havelis that once housed merchant families now house pigeons and legal disputes.

I find the address. It's a real estate office now. The haveli they bought — the one this story is about — belongs to someone else.

Devika and Arun meet me at a cafe. They still live in Jaipur. They just don't own a haveli anymore.

Devika was a graphic designer. Arun worked in hospitality management.

They found the haveli on a weekend trip. 200 years old. Carved jharokhas. A courtyard with a dried-up fountain.

Rs. 45 lakh. "A steal," the broker said.

It was. Just not for them.

Renovation estimate: Rs. 30 lakh.
Actual cost: Rs. 92 lakh. And counting.

Heritage regulations meant they couldn't touch the facade. Couldn't add modern plumbing without committee approval. The approval took 8 months.

Eight months of paying EMI on a building they couldn't use.

The contractor vanished twice. The second time with Rs. 3 lakh of advance.

They opened with 4 rooms. The third floor was unfinished — no money left.

First month: 3 bookings. Tourist season.

Second month: 1 booking. Off-season.

They hadn't modeled for seasonality. Jaipur's tourist window is October to March. That's six months. The other six, the city empties.

Then the Airbnb reviews started.

"Construction noise from next door." "Plumbing issues in Room 2." "Beautiful but not functional."

3.2 stars.

Two years. That's how long they lasted.

The loan EMI was Rs. 78,000 a month. Revenue in off-season: Rs. 20,000.

They sold the haveli to a real estate investor. At a loss.

The investor didn't want to run a homestay. He wanted the land.

The carved jharokhas, the courtyard, the fountain — he didn't care about any of it.

Devika cried that day. Not for the money. For the jharokhas.

They fell in love with the Instagram version of their business.

The aesthetic. The reviews. The "living in a haveli" dream.

The actual struggle was plumbing permits, contractor management, seasonal cash flow, and heritage committee bureaucracy.

They didn't sign up for that.

The business they imagined and the business they got were two completely different things.

One existed on a mood board. The other existed in a heritage committee's filing cabinet.

Next stop: Anand.

A small town in Gujarat where a farmer got tired of watching middlemen pay his neighbours nothing.

He organized 30 families into a dairy cooperative.

The refrigeration truck broke down one summer. The milk adulteration accusations came from a rival.

But the sweet shop down the road tasted the difference.

episodes.synopsis: In Jaipur, a couple buys a crumbling haveli to turn into a boutique heritage homestay. Renovation costs triple, heritage regulations block modern plumbing, tourist season is shorter than expected, Airbnb reviews tank, and they can't finish the third floor. They sell at a loss after two years, still paying the renovation loan.
episodes.caption: Ever fallen in love with the idea of a business but not the actual work of running it? Jaipur has a lot of havelis with similar stories.

episodes.title: The Milk Run

slides.text: The Milk Run

Anand doesn't look like a revolution.

Flat roads. White cattle. Milk cans stacked outside every third house.

But behind one of these houses, a farmer built something that 30 families now depend on.

He wasn't trying to build a business. He was trying to stop getting cheated.

For years, a middleman collected milk from the village.

Paid Rs. 18 per liter. Sold it for Rs. 42.

Farmers knew the math. Nobody did anything.

Ramesh did. He went door to door — 30 families — and said: "What if we sell it ourselves?"

The rival collector started a rumor.

"Their milk is adulterated. Don't buy from them."

12 families panicked. 6 left the cooperative within a week.

Ramesh spent three days getting his milk tested at a government lab.

Results came back clean. But by then, 6 families were gone.

Then the refrigeration truck broke down.

June. 42 degrees.

800 liters of milk. No cooling. No backup.

Two days of collection — spoiled.

Ramesh couldn't pay the remaining families that week.

Three more left.

The bank said no.

"Farmer cooperative" didn't fit their loan categories.

No collateral. No audited books. No track record.

Ramesh fixed the truck with borrowed money from his brother-in-law.

He had 21 families left. Down from 30.

A local sweet shop chain needed a reliable milk supplier.

Their current one was inconsistent. Some days watered down.

The owner tasted Ramesh's milk.

Then tasted it again.

"How much can you supply daily?"

That one contract gave 21 families a guaranteed buyer.

Ramesh wasn't building a business.

He was tired of watching middlemen pay his neighbors nothing.

The struggle of convincing farmers to trust a collective — to wait for monthly payments instead of daily cash — he understood it.

Because he lived it.

That's the only reason he could endure it.

Next on Before The Signboard:

Lucknow. A family that's been making kebabs for four generations.

The youngest son wanted to put them in a restaurant.

His grandfather called it betrayal.

episodes.synopsis: A farmer in Anand organized 30 families into a small dairy cooperative. Faced adulteration accusations, members leaving, a broken refrigeration truck, and a bank that wouldn't lend. A local sweet shop chain tasting the difference changed everything.
episodes.caption: Ever tried organizing people who've been burned by every promise before yours? That's the real cooperative.

episodes.title: Four Generations Over A Sigri

slides.text: Four Generations Over A Sigri

Old Lucknow smells like smoke and ghee before you see it.

Narrow lanes. Charcoal sigris glowing outside every third shop.

Somewhere in this maze, a family has been cooking kebabs since before independence.

The youngest son put them on a plate with cutlery.

His elders called it a crime.

Imran grew up standing over a sigri.

12-hour shifts. Fanning coal. Learning the exact moment to pull the seekh.

His father did it. His grandfather did it. His great-grandfather did it.

But Imran wanted tables. A menu. A billing machine.

His grandfather said: "You're selling our izzat for a cash register."

He opened anyway. Small place near Hazratganj.

First month: 8-10 customers a day.

Rent was built for 80.

Second month: kitchen fire. Gas line. The tandoor wall caught.

Insurance didn't cover a rented kitchen.

He rebuilt it with money meant for his sister's wedding.

Staff stole ingredients. Meat is expensive.

He caught his cook packing mutton into a bag at closing.

Fired him. Cooked alone for two weeks.

14 hours on the sigri. Then cleaned the restaurant. Then did the books.

He lost 4 kilos that month.

He tried a second location. Consistency collapsed.

The kebabs tasted different. Customers noticed.

"This isn't like the original."

Of course it wasn't. The original had Imran's hands.

He shut the second location in 3 months.

Back to one kitchen. Back to the sigri.

A food blogger walked in on a Tuesday.

Shot a 90-second reel. Posted it.

2.3 million views.

Two-month waitlist by Friday.

But Imran didn't open a second location.

Not until he'd spent 8 months training a second chef who could taste what he tasted.

His family made kebabs for four generations.

The struggle of standing over a sigri for 12 hours — he didn't choose it. It chose him.

What nearly killed the business wasn't the cooking.

It was everything around it — rent, staff, consistency.

The kebabs were never the problem.

Next on Before The Signboard:

Indore. A street food vendor's son who believed his father's mixture deserved more than one corner.

His father said: "My food doesn't need a packet."

The first batch went stale in 10 days.

episodes.synopsis: A chef from a family of cooks in old Lucknow wanted to bring Lucknowi kebabs to a modern restaurant format. Family elders called it betrayal. Terrible footfall, a kitchen fire, staff theft, and consistency problems nearly killed it. A viral food reel changed everything — but he only expanded when the food could survive without him.
episodes.caption: Some businesses fail because of the product. Some fail because of everything around the product. Know which fight you're in.

episodes.title: The Packet

slides.text: The Packet

Indore runs on street food.

Every corner has a cart. Every cart has a crowd.

But one cart on Sarafa Bazaar had a line that wrapped around the block.

28 years. Same spot. Same recipe. Same man.

His son thought: what if the food could travel?

Vikram grew up behind that cart.

He knew the mixture by smell — the exact moment the sev was right, the ratio of peanuts to chivda.

But he also watched his father stand 10 hours a day, six days a week, for 28 years.

Same corner. Same income. Same ceiling.

"The food is worth more than one corner," Vikram said.

His father said: "My food doesn't need a packet."

FSSAI licensing took 7 months.

Four visits to the office. Wrong forms. Missing documents. A bribe request he refused.

By the time the license came, he'd already spent Rs. 80,000 on packaging that didn't work.

The first batch — 500 packets — went stale in 10 days.

Every single one returned.

Retailers laughed.

"Unknown brand? No TV ad? No distributor?

We'll give you shelf space when Haldiram's gives it up."

Vikram left his packets at 15 shops on consignment.

12 returned them untouched after a month.

The other 3 never called back.

A food scientist at a local college agreed to help.

Nitrogen flushing. Modified atmosphere packaging. Moisture barrier film.

Shelf life went from 10 days to 4 months.

Vikram didn't go back to retailers.

He went to railway station kiosks.

3 kiosks. Travelers bought it. Carried it home. Told people.

The product started traveling before the brand did.

Orders came from Bhopal. Then Nagpur. Then Ahmedabad.

People who'd tasted it on a train wanted it at home.

Vikram's father watched the orders pile up.

He didn't say he was proud.

But he started coming to the warehouse on Sundays. Checking the seasoning.

His father's mixture was legendary on one corner.

The son's struggle wasn't making food.

It was making it survive a supply chain.

Packaging. Shelf life. Distribution. Licensing.

A completely different skill.

He learned it because he believed the food deserved to travel.

Next on Before The Signboard:

Kochi. A young man saw a YouTube video about houseboat revenue.

Rs. 15,000 per day per boat.

He didn't see the diesel costs. The monsoons. The 200 other people who watched the same video.

episodes.synopsis: A street food vendor's son wanted to package his father's famous mixture and sell it beyond the cart. FSSAI licensing, bad packaging, retailer rejection, and a father who felt insulted nearly ended it. A food scientist and three railway kiosks changed the trajectory.
episodes.caption: The product was always good. The real skill was making it survive without you standing next to it.

episodes.title: The Same YouTube Video

slides.text: The Same YouTube Video

The backwaters look like a screensaver.

Green water. Palm trees. Wooden boats drifting slow.

But count the houseboats.

Keep counting.

200. Maybe more.

Most of them running the same route, same menu, same Instagram photos.

One of them used to belong to a man named Deepak.

Deepak was 26. Working IT support in Kochi.

He watched a YouTube video one night.

"Houseboat business in Kerala — Rs. 15,000/day revenue."

The comments were full of people saying: "Bro, best passive income."

He didn't read the replies from people who'd actually tried it.

He took a Rs. 18 lakh loan. Bought a decommissioned rice barge. Converted it.

Opened in October. Peak season.

First two months were decent. 60% occupancy.

Then monsoon hit.

June through October — five months — bookings dropped to near zero.

The loan EMI didn't drop.

Tourists complained about the water.

Pollution. Sewage smell in some stretches.

"This doesn't look like the photos."

Two-star reviews stacked up.

Deepak had no control over the backwaters. He just floated on them.

Then the engine started failing. Repairs cost Rs. 40,000 each time.

Diesel alone was Rs. 2,500 a day.

A tourist slipped on the deck. Fractured his wrist.

Filed a legal case.

Deepak didn't have liability insurance. He didn't even know it existed.

The legal fees were Rs. 1.5 lakh. The case is still open.

He sold the boat for Rs. 9 lakh — half what he paid.

Still owes Rs. 11 lakh on the loan.

He saw a YouTube video about houseboat revenue and jumped in.

He chose "Rs. 15,000 per day per boat."

The struggle was diesel costs. Tourist safety. Monsoon survival.

Competing with everyone who watched the same video.

No connection to water. No love for hospitality.

Just the math.

The math was wrong.

Next on Before The Signboard:

Pune. A couple who started a school because they hated how their own kids were being taught.

7 students the first year. They needed 40 to survive.

It took 5 years to fill a classroom.

episodes.synopsis: A young man took a loan to convert a rice barge into a tourist houseboat in Alleppey. Monsoons, pollution complaints, 200 identical competitors, engine problems, and a tourist injury led to selling at half price in 18 months. He's still in court.
episodes.caption: Revenue per day looks great on a spreadsheet. Nobody puts the monsoon on a spreadsheet.

episodes.title: The First Classroom

slides.text: The First Classroom

The school doesn't look like one.

An old bungalow. Repainted walls. A hand-painted sign.

The playground is the driveway.

But inside, 23 kids are doing something I haven't seen in any school I've visited.

They're asking questions. Out loud. Without raising their hands.

This is year one. And it almost didn't survive.

Meera and Sunil were both teachers. 12 years each.

Meera taught English at a CBSE school. Sunil taught math at an ICSE one.

Both watched their own kids come home from school hating learning.

Rote memorization. Punishment for wrong answers. Homework that meant nothing.

"If we can't find the right school," Meera said, "we'll build one."

They rented the bungalow. Painted it themselves. Bought second-hand desks.

Put out flyers in the neighborhood.

Admission target: 40 students.

Enrollments by June: 7.

Seven kids. In a city with a million parents.

Two of those seven were their own children.

Parents came. Looked around. Left.

"Where's the computer lab?"
"You don't have a school bus?"
"What's your board percentage track record?"

Track record. They'd been open for 3 weeks.

One mother said: "I can't risk my child on an experiment."

That word — experiment — stayed with Meera for months.

Their only hired teacher quit after a month.

"I got an offer from DPS. Sorry."

Meera took over English, Hindi, and EVS.
Sunil took math, science, and sports.

They taught from 8 AM to 2 PM. Did admin until 6. Called parents until 8.

Then the education board inspector showed up.

"Inadequate facilities. You have 60 days to comply or we shut you down."

They borrowed from Sunil's father. Fixed what the board demanded.

By December, word had spread. Slowly.

A parent whose kid loved coming to school told another parent.

That parent told two more.

End of year one: 23 students.

Still losing Rs. 45,000 a month.

Sunil said: "We should stop. We tried."

Meera said: "No."

Building a school isn't an education problem.

It's a trust problem.

And trust takes longer than money.

Meera knew this. Sunil knew this.

But knowing it doesn't make the bank balance hurt less.

Part 2 — next week:

What happened when they finally got to 200 students.

And realized that was a whole new set of problems.

episodes.synopsis: A couple — both former teachers — started a school in a Pune suburb because they hated how their own kids were being taught. 7 enrollments year one. Parents didn't trust a new school. A teacher quit. The education board nearly shut them down. Part 1 ends with 23 students, still losing money, and a marriage being tested.
episodes.caption: Trust takes longer than money. Every new school, clinic, and restaurant learns this the hard way.

episodes.title: The School That Almost Broke Them — Part 2

slides.text: The School That Almost Broke Them — Part 2

I came back to Pune.

Same suburb. Same bungalow-turned-school.

Except now there's a proper gate, a painted sign, and 200 kids inside.

She looked more tired than last time. He looked angrier.

200 students meant 200 families.

And families have opinions.

A group of parents formed a WhatsApp committee. They had suggestions about the curriculum, the teachers, the lunch menu, the annual day budget.

Suggestions that sounded a lot like demands.

Then a teacher was accused of favoritism.

One parent said her child was being ignored.

Another said the teacher gave extra attention to "donation parents."

Neither was true. But truth doesn't matter in a WhatsApp group with 180 members.

A competing school opened 2 km away.

AC classrooms. Smart boards. A swimming pool.

Their school had ceiling fans and a playground that was mostly mud.

15 families left in one term.

The marriage was cracking.

He ran operations — buses, fees, maintenance.
She ran academics — curriculum, teachers, students.

They stopped agreeing on anything.

At home, they argued about the school.
At school, they argued about home.

The staff could hear them through the office wall.

Then a kid fell on the playground.

Broken arm. Parents were called. An ambulance came.

Within 48 hours, a group of 30 families had a letter ready.

"Unsafe premises. We're pulling our children out unless..."

The list of demands was two pages long.

But then the first batch graduated.

Board exam results came in. Their students scored well.

But that wasn't what saved them.

It was what the parents saw.

Kids who asked questions. Who were curious. Who weren't afraid of teachers.

One mother said: "My son argues with me now. With logic. I don't know whether to be proud or terrified."

Those parents became evangelists.

They chose the struggle of shaping children.

Not the struggle of running an institution.

The institution problems — politics, competition, money, marriage — nearly destroyed them.

But the kids kept them going.

Because that was the struggle they signed up for.

Next stop: Tirupur.

A man moved from Bangalore with a spreadsheet and a plan to crack garment exports.

Tirupur has everything — dyers, stitchers, shipping agents.

He had none of them.

episodes.synopsis: The school has 200 students after year 4. But scale brought problems they never imagined — parent politics, teacher accusations, a competing school, a marriage cracking under pressure, and a playground injury that nearly emptied half their classrooms.
episodes.caption: They built a school. Then the school almost broke their marriage. What keeps you going when the thing you built starts breaking you?

episodes.title: The Spreadsheet and the Stitchers

slides.text: The Spreadsheet and the Stitchers

Tirupur smells like dye.

Every street has a unit. Stitching, dyeing, pressing, packing.

The man I'm looking for shut his down eight months ago.

He's back in Bangalore now. He agreed to talk on the phone.

His voice was flat. Not angry. Just flat.

He'd worked in supply chain at a Bangalore apparel company for six years.

Knew the numbers cold. Margins, MOQs, shipping timelines.

So he moved to Tirupur.

"Everything is here. Dyers, stitchers, fabric mills, shipping agents. How hard can it be?"

His first international buyer ordered 5,000 polo shirts.

He sourced fabric. Hired stitchers. Set up a rented unit.

The shipment was rejected.

Stitching inconsistency. Collar alignment off by 3mm on 40% of the batch.

The buyer didn't ask for a redo. They just cancelled.

He needed more workers to meet the next MOQ.

But workers in Tirupur know their worth.

They wanted established-factory wages. PF. Overtime.

He was a one-order startup offering "growth potential."

They laughed. Politely. But they laughed.

He landed a second buyer. Smaller order. He was careful this time.

Shipped the container.

Customs held it for three weeks. Paperwork issue.

By the time it cleared, the buyer had sourced from someone else.

The container sat in a yard. The dye lots across batches didn't even match.

He couldn't resell it.

Tirupur's ecosystem works for people who grew up in it.

Who know the dyers by name. Who drink chai with the shipping agents. Whose fathers taught them which stitcher is reliable at 2 AM before a deadline.

He moved from Bangalore with a spreadsheet.

The struggle of garment manufacturing is relationships, not logistics.

He didn't have them. And you can't build twenty years of trust in eleven months.

Next stop: Varanasi.

A fourth-generation weaver who almost left for a call center.

Every weaver his age did leave.

He stayed. And the loom almost starved him before it saved him.

episodes.synopsis: A man moved from Bangalore to Tirupur to start a garment export unit, banking on the city's ecosystem. He had the numbers. He didn't have the relationships. Closed in 11 months.
episodes.caption: He had the data. He had the plan. He didn't have twenty years of chai with the right people. Ever walked into an industry where the real infrastructure is invisible?

episodes.title: The Loom He Couldn't Leave

slides.text: The Loom He Couldn't Leave

The lanes of Varanasi don't let you walk straight.

I followed the sound of a shuttle through a doorway so narrow I had to turn sideways.

Upstairs, in a room smaller than most kitchens, a man sat at a handloom.

His fingers moved faster than I could follow.

He's 28. He's been weaving since he was 12.

When he was 22, he almost took a call center job in Noida.

Rs. 14,000 a month. AC office. Regular salary.

His father was making Rs. 8,000 from the loom. Some months less.

Every weaver his age had already left.

He packed a bag. Got to the bus station.

Came back.

He stayed. And the problems stayed with him.

Power looms were producing "Banarasi" silk at a third of the price.

Customers couldn't tell the difference. Or didn't care.

Handloom margins collapsed. His father worked 14-hour days to make what a power loom made in 2.

The middleman was the real cage.

One trader controlled access to every buyer in the market.

He set the prices. Took 40% commission. Paid when he felt like it.

Every weaver in the lane worked for this one man.

And nobody complained. Because he was the only door to the market.

He decided to go direct. Built a website.

His father called it foolish. "Who buys sarees from a computer?"

He spent his savings on photos, a domain, a basic site.

Six months. Zero orders.

Not one.

The middleman heard about the website and cut his father's commission to 50%.

Punishment.

Month seven.

An email.

A fashion designer from Mumbai had found the website. She wanted 40 dupattas for a runway show.

Specific colors. Specific weave patterns. Tight deadline.

He wove for 20 hours a day for three weeks. His father helped. Didn't say a word about the website.

The show happened. The designer posted photos.

Three more designers called that month.

He could have left. Every weaver his age did.

He stayed because the loom was the only place his hands felt right.

The struggle of fighting middlemen, convincing his father, waiting six months for a market that might never come —

He endured it because leaving felt worse.

That's not a business plan.

That's the only honest reason any of this works.

Next stop: Chandigarh.

A pathologist who chose a rented shop over a hospital salary.

He spent three years proving his reports were better.

Most of those years, he proved it for free.

episodes.synopsis: A fourth-generation weaver who almost left for a call center job stayed to modernize the family workshop. He fought middlemen, his father, and a dying market. A fashion designer's runway order changed everything.
episodes.caption: He couldn't explain why he came back from the bus station. Some struggles choose you. What's the thing you can't walk away from?

episodes.title: Trust in the Blood

slides.text: Trust in the Blood

Chandigarh is a city that runs on order.

Sectors. Grid roads. Everything planned.

In Sector 22, between a tailor and a sweet shop, there's a diagnostic lab.

Small. Clean. Unremarkable from outside.

Inside, the machines are better than most hospital labs in the city.

The man who built this started with one microscope and a rented room.

He was a pathologist. MD. Could have joined any hospital.

Good salary. Predictable hours. Pension.

Instead, he rented a 200 sq ft shop and bought a second-hand analyzer.

"I wanted my name on the report. Not someone else's letterhead."

His family thought he was having a crisis.

He visited every clinic in four sectors.

"Send your patients to my lab. My reports will be faster and more accurate."

Doctors smiled politely.

Nobody sent anyone.

They had arrangements with established chains. Commissions. Referral fees.

He was offering better science.

They wanted better margins.

Month five.

A patient's liver function test came back abnormal. Severely abnormal.

He flagged it. Called the patient. Recommended immediate follow-up.

The hospital re-tested. Normal.

False positive. His report was wrong.

The patient's family wanted to sue.

"We almost started treatment based on your report. Do you know what that could have done?"

Equipment maintenance alone cost more than his rent.

He couldn't afford a second technician.

So he did everything.

Collections at 7 AM. Testing until 2 PM. Reports until 6 PM. Cleaning and calibration until 9 PM.

Seven days a week. For a year.

His wife left dinner on the table. Most nights he ate it cold.

He started doing free health camps.

Every Sunday. A different housing society.

Cholesterol. Blood sugar. Basic panels.

Free. No catch. Just his name on the report.

"If the report is good, remember the lab."

Week after week. Society after society.

People started coming in on their own.

Then they started asking their doctors to send reports to his lab.

Three years in, the doctors stopped resisting.

Because their patients weren't asking anymore. They were insisting.

A diagnostic lab sells accuracy you can trust with your life.

The struggle isn't science. It's convincing people to trust a new name with their blood reports.

He chose that struggle because he believed his reports were better.

And he was willing to prove it for free.

For years.

That's not marketing. That's conviction wearing a white coat.

Next stop: Belgaum.

A retired government officer who thought jaggery would be a quiet retirement project.

Passive income. How hard can sugarcane be?

He found out.

episodes.synopsis: A pathologist started a diagnostic lab in a rented shop instead of joining a hospital. Doctors wouldn't refer. A false positive nearly became a lawsuit. He built trust patient by patient, free camp by free camp, for three years.
episodes.caption: He gave away thousands of free tests to build a name people trusted with their health. What's something you'd prove for free just because you believed in it?

episodes.title: The Retirement That Wasn't

slides.text: The Retirement That Wasn't

Belgaum sits where Karnataka meets Maharashtra.

Sugarcane everywhere. The air smells sweet near the processing units.

I found him at home. Not at a factory. Not at a field.

The factory is gone. The equipment sold.

He's 63. He offered me chai and spoke like a man who's rehearsed this story to himself a hundred times.

35 years in the revenue department.

He retired with a pension, savings, and a plan.

Belgaum makes jaggery. Everyone makes jaggery.

"I'll set up a processing unit. Buy sugarcane, make jaggery, sell it. Steady income. Passive."

He said that word — passive — three times.

Each time with more bitterness.

The first problem: sugarcane supply.

Farmers sell to whoever shows up first with cash.

He'd placed orders. Signed agreements.

The agreements meant nothing.

A bigger processor offered Rs. 50 more per ton. His farmers vanished overnight.

No sugarcane. No jaggery. No income.

Just a processing unit sitting empty in harvest season.

When he did get sugarcane, timing was everything.

Process too early — the jaggery is pale, low quality.
Process too late — the cane has dried, yield drops.

He hired workers. But harvest season is harvest season.

Every farm, every factory, every unit needs labor at the same time.

His workers showed up when they felt like it.

Some days he ran the boilers himself. A 63-year-old man. Standing over a vat at 4 AM.

His jaggery was good. Pure. No chemicals.

The market didn't care.

Cheaper jaggery — laced with chemicals for color and shelf life — sold at half the price.

Retailers wouldn't stock his. "Too expensive. Customers won't pay."

Then the warehouse fire.

An electrical short. Half his first season's stock — gone.

No insurance. He hadn't thought of it.

Why would he? It was supposed to be passive.

He saw jaggery as a retirement project.

Passive income. "How hard can sugarcane be?"

The struggle was agricultural. Seasonal. Labor-intensive. Unforgiving.

He chose the outcome — steady retirement income.

And got a full-time crisis.

Two seasons. Most of his savings. Gone.

You can't retire into a struggle you've never lived.

Next stop: Nagpur.

An engineer who quit his job to solve cold chain logistics for farmers.

His first shipment of oranges rotted on a highway at 2 AM.

That story takes two episodes to tell.

episodes.synopsis: A retired government officer invested his retirement savings in jaggery processing. He saw passive income. He got agricultural, seasonal, labor-intensive reality. Lost most of his savings in two seasons.
episodes.caption: He worked 35 years for a safe retirement. Then bet it on "how hard can it be?" What's a decision you made that looked simple from the outside?

episodes.title: The Highway at 2 AM — Part 1

slides.text: The Highway at 2 AM — Part 1

I found him at a warehouse on the Nagpur-Pune highway.

Four refrigerated trucks parked outside. A team loading crates of oranges at 5 AM.

He was checking temperatures on his phone. Every truck. Every crate.

"This obsession started the night I lost 3 tonnes of oranges on this same road."

He'd spent 6 years at an MNC logistics company. Supply chain optimization. Route planning. Cold storage analytics.

He knew exactly how much produce rotted between Indian farms and markets.

40%.

He had the PowerPoint to prove it.

So he quit to fix it.

No farmer trusted a guy with a PowerPoint.

"Bhai, yeh cold chain kya hota hai? Hum toh aaj todke kal bechte hain."

He visited 50 farms in 3 months.

47 said no.

3 said "show me first."

His first refrigerated truck was a converted tempo.

Bought second-hand. Fitted a cooling unit from a scrapped container.

It broke down every other week.

Then the night that changed everything.

Nagpur-Amravati highway. 2 AM. Cooling unit died.

3 tonnes of oranges. Rotting in real time.

No mechanic for 50 kilometers.

He lost the entire shipment.

The 3 farmers who'd trusted him?

"We told you. Sell same day. No need for your fancy truck."

His partner — a college friend who'd put in half the seed money — pulled out.

Took Rs. 8 lakhs. Left a WhatsApp message.

"Bhai, this isn't going to work. Sorry."

Investors laughed.

"Cold chain in Vidarbha? For oranges? The margins don't work."

He pitched 11 times. Got rejected 11 times.

Meanwhile — his wife was pregnant.

Savings at Rs. 1.2 lakhs. One truck. Three reluctant farmers.

His old company called. "Position's still open. Come back."

He almost said yes.

Every logistics founder talks about "solving problems."

But the problem was on a highway at 2 AM.

With rotting oranges and no mechanic for 50 km.

That's the actual struggle.

Slides don't prepare you for it.
Investor decks don't mention it.
LinkedIn posts skip that part.

The question isn't whether you have a solution.

It's whether you can stand on that highway and not quit.

Part 2 — next week.

APMC reforms changed the game.

Farmers could suddenly sell directly.

They needed cold chain. They needed him.

But demand you can't meet is just a different kind of failure.

He wasn't ready.

episodes.synopsis: An engineer who quit his MNC logistics job to solve last-mile cold chain for farmers around Nagpur. Part 1 covers the brutal early days — broken trucks, rotting oranges, a partner who walked away with half the seed money, and a pregnant wife watching the savings disappear.
episodes.caption: Everyone wants to "solve supply chain problems." Nobody talks about what happens at 2 AM on an empty highway when the solution breaks down.

episodes.title: The Highway at 2 AM — Part 2

slides.text: The Highway at 2 AM — Part 2

Same warehouse. Same highway.

But now there were four trucks, not one.

A whiteboard with routes. A small team tracking temperatures.

"Everyone thinks the APMC reforms saved me," he said.

"They almost killed me faster."

APMC reforms hit like a flood.

Farmers could now sell directly to buyers. No mandatory mandi.

But direct selling meant transport. And transport for perishables meant cold chain.

His phone rang non-stop.

"Bhai, 5 tonnes Nagpur to Mumbai. Kal subah tak chahiye."

He had one working truck.

He borrowed to buy a second truck. Then a third.

Hired drivers who'd never handled refrigerated cargo.

One driver left the cooling unit off for 200 km because "it was making noise."

Another shipment lost.

He needed 10 trucks but could afford 2.

The gap between demand and capacity was eating him alive.

A pharma company approached him.

"We need cold chain for vaccines. Nagpur to 12 district towns."

The contract would've tripled his revenue.

But they needed ISO certification. Temperature logs. Insurance.

He had a WhatsApp group and a notebook.

He said yes anyway.

Failed the audit in week three.

Debt was piling up.

Two new trucks on EMI.
Drivers' salaries.
Diesel costs he hadn't projected.

He was running 5 routes badly instead of 1 route well.

His wife — the one who'd stayed silent through the rotting oranges — finally spoke.

"You're doing the same thing again. Too much, too fast. Pick one road and own it."

He stopped.

Dropped 4 routes. Kept one.

Nagpur to Pune. 600 km. One corridor.

Every farmer on that route got guaranteed pickup.
Every truck maintained the exact temperature.
Every delivery arrived on time.

Reliability on one road.

Other routes came back — on his terms, when he was ready.

The first struggle was survival.

The second was discipline — saying no to growth when growth could kill you.

He endured both.

Because the rotting oranges on that highway never left his mind.

Every truck he runs, every temperature he checks at 5 AM — it all goes back to that night.

The highway at 2 AM made him.

The discipline to stay on one road saved him.

Next stop — Dehradun.

An IIM graduate who left consulting to grow organic rice in the Doon Valley.

"Meaningful work," he called it.

The soil had a different word for it.

episodes.synopsis: Continuation. APMC reforms created sudden demand for cold chain. He went from survival mode to scaling mode — and almost drowned in growth. The turning point: saying no to expansion and perfecting one route.
episodes.caption: Survival is one struggle. Saying no to growth is another. Most founders only prepare for the first.

episodes.title: The Meaningful Pivot

slides.text: The Meaningful Pivot

I met him at a cafe in Rajpur Road.

Not a farm. A cafe.

He was back in consulting. Remote. Dehradun was now just a nice place to live.

"The brand still exists," he said, showing me the Instagram page.

412 followers. Last post: 14 months ago.

He was 28 when he quit.

McKinsey-style consulting. Good money. No meaning.

"I'd write decks about sustainability for clients who didn't care. I wanted to actually do it."

Organic farming in the Doon Valley.

He'd read about it. Watched documentaries. Visited two farms.

That was his due diligence.

Organic certification requires 3 years of chemical-free land.

He leased 4 acres from a farmer who swore no chemicals.

Certification inspection: soil test showed pesticide residue.

18 months of paperwork. Wasted.

"The farmer didn't lie," he said. "He just didn't count the pesticide his neighbor's field drained into ours."

Yields were 40% lower than conventional rice.

He'd budgeted for 20% lower.

Customers wanted organic.

But not at Rs. 180/kg when normal rice was Rs. 60.

"Everyone says they'll pay for organic. Put a 3x price tag on it and watch them pick up the regular bag."

Two years in.

Savings: gone.
Certification: still pending.
Customer base: 40 families on a WhatsApp group.
Revenue: Rs. 3 lakhs total. Over two years.

His parents stopped asking how the farm was going.

That's when he knew.

He opened his laptop and updated his LinkedIn.

He wanted to "do something meaningful."

Organic farming looked meaningful from a consulting deck.

The actual struggle was soil chemistry. Weather patterns. A market that says it wants organic but won't pay 3x for rice.

He chose the story, not the struggle.

The story was beautiful — IIM grad becomes organic farmer.

The struggle was ugly — failed soil tests, 40% lower yields, and 40 customers in two years.

He signed up for the Instagram version of farming.

The farm needed someone who'd sign up for the dirt.

Next stop — Hyderabad.

A home cook whose biryani went viral on WhatsApp.

She turned her apartment into a cloud kitchen.

Everyone said, "Low investment, high returns."

Nobody mentioned the 4 AM prep. The burns. The 1-star reviews.

Or the kitchen fire.

episodes.synopsis: An IIM graduate who left consulting to start an organic farming brand in the Doon Valley. Certification delays, low yields, skeptical customers, and a contamination scare. Back in consulting after two years. The brand exists on paper. The fields don't.
episodes.caption: "I want to do something meaningful." Everyone says it. But meaningful work isn't chosen for its meaning. It's chosen for its struggle. And the struggle better be one you actually want.

episodes.title: The 4 AM Biryani

slides.text: The 4 AM Biryani

I found her kitchen before I found her.

The smell hit from the staircase. Dum biryani. Slow-cooked. The real kind.

She was on the phone, managing a delivery, while stirring a pot with her other hand.

No fancy setup. Two commercial burners. A husband packing orders at the dining table.

"Sit. Eat first. Then we'll talk."

It started with WhatsApp.

She'd share recipes in neighborhood aunty groups. Photos of her biryani.

"Arre yeh bech kyun nahi deti?"

She laughed it off the first ten times.

The eleventh time, she made 15 plates. Sold them in 2 hours.

Her husband was still employed then. This was "timepass."

Until he lost his job.

She listed on Zomato and Swiggy.

Orders jumped to 40 a day. Then 60.

Then she saw the commission structure.

30% to the platform. Payment after 7 days.

She was cooking 60 biryanis a day and the apps were making more per plate than she was.

"I'm their kitchen. They're my landlord. And the rent is 30%."

Then the review.

1 star. "Found hair in biryani."

It was a strand of basil. Tulsi. She'd been experimenting with a new recipe.

But a 1-star review on Swiggy isn't a conversation. It's a verdict.

Her rating dropped from 4.6 to 4.1.

Orders halved in two weeks.

Two months to recover what one photo destroyed.

Her husband quit his next job to help full-time.

Both incomes now on biryani.

They scaled to 80 orders. Quality slipped. Complaints rose.

Then the fire.

An oil spill near the burner. Kitchen wall caught.

No one was hurt. But the kitchen was gone for 3 weeks.

3 weeks of zero income. Both of them. No backup.

Neighbors complained to the housing society.

"Commercial cooking is not allowed in residential flats."

She rebuilt. Moved to a rented commercial space. Smaller. Legitimate.

And changed the model completely.

Subscription biryani. Weekly office orders.

Predictable demand. No platform commission. Repeat customers who paid directly.

Zomato and Swiggy became marketing — not the business.

She controls the relationship now. Not an algorithm.

"Just start a cloud kitchen. Low investment."

The investment isn't money.

It's your reputation on every plate.

She endured it because cooking for people was never work.

The 4 AM prep. The burns. The 1-star reviews. The fire.

That's what she signed up for.

Not because she chose it — because she couldn't imagine doing anything else.

The biryani was never the business plan.

It was the only thing she knew how to do when everything else fell apart.

Next stop — Rajkot.

10,000 engineering workshops in one city.

A toolmaker who bet everything on precision nobody else wanted to bother with.

0.01 mm tolerances. Not glamorous. Not scalable.

Just perfect.

episodes.synopsis: A home cook whose biryani recipes went viral on WhatsApp groups. She turned her apartment into a cloud kitchen, survived platform commissions, a rating disaster, a kitchen fire, and found a model that worked — on her terms.
episodes.caption: "Low investment, high returns." That's what they say about cloud kitchens. Nobody mentions the part where your reputation lives inside a stranger's 1-star review.

episodes.title: The 0.01mm Man

slides.text: The 0.01mm Man

His workshop was in an industrial estate off the Gondal road.

Small. Clean. Quieter than the workshops next door.

A CNC machine humming in the corner. Digital calipers on every surface.

He picked up a finished part — a valve component — and held it like it was made of glass.

"This is 0.01mm from perfect. That's too much. We'll redo it."

He grew up in a workshop.

His father made pump components. Basic turning. Decent margins in the 90s.

By 2010, Rajkot had 10,000 workshops doing the same thing.

Price wars. 5% margins. Race to the bottom.

His father's advice: "Get a government job."

He bought a CNC machine on EMI instead.

The CNC machine was his entire bet.

Rs. 18 lakhs. EMI: Rs. 42,000/month.

First big order: 500 valve bodies for a pump manufacturer.

Defective batch. Tolerance off by 0.05mm.

The client rejected everything.

500 parts. Scrap metal.

Rs. 3.5 lakhs gone. EMI still due.

He trained 3 operators over 6 months.

All three left for Gulf jobs within a year.

Higher pay. Better conditions. Can't compete with Dubai.

Every time he trained someone, he was training them to leave.

Electricity cuts didn't help.

A power outage mid-machining run ruins the part. Every time.

Rajkot's grid wasn't built for precision work.

He bought a generator. Another EMI.

Then the competitor.

A bigger workshop started undercutting him by 15% on every tender.

Same parts. Lower price. Faster delivery.

He couldn't match it without cutting corners.

So he stopped competing.

Not quit. Stopped competing on the same parts.

He looked at what the bigger shops wouldn't bother with.

High-precision, low-volume. Custom parts. Tolerances of 0.01mm.

The work nobody wanted because it was slow, difficult, and couldn't scale.

He became the go-to for work that required perfection.

Diesel engine components with tolerances bigger shops couldn't be bothered with.

Pump parts that needed custom machining.

One client. Then five. Then twenty.

Margins improved. Not because he raised prices.

Because no one else was competing.

When you're the only one who does the hard thing, you set the terms.

Rajkot has 10,000 workshops.

He survived because he'd rather get one part perfect than rush a hundred.

The struggle of precision — rejected batches, 0.01mm tolerances, operators who leave, power cuts that destroy runs.

He loved that struggle.

Business problems were noise. The lathe was the signal.

He didn't build a business around a market gap.

He built one around the only thing he couldn't stop doing — making perfect parts.

The gap found him.

Next stop — Amritsar.

A woman who turned Punjabi weddings into a business.

Big fat Indian weddings. Bigger expectations.

The fattest margins she'd ever seen — until the groom's mother changed the menu 48 hours before the sangeet.

That's the actual job.

episodes.synopsis: A toolmaker in Rajkot who started a precision engineering workshop for the pump and diesel engine industry. In a city of 10,000 workshops, he survived by specializing in tolerance levels nobody else wanted to bother with.
episodes.caption: 10,000 workshops in one city. All competing on price. One man who stopped competing and started perfecting. Sometimes the niche finds you.

episodes.title: The Last Dance

slides.text: The Last Dance

I find her at a wedding venue on GT Road.

She's not the planner anymore. She's the coordinator. Employee badge. Walkie-talkie.

She used to run the show.

Now she runs someone else's checklist.

It started with her cousin's wedding.

She planned the whole thing — decor, caterer, DJ, mehndi night, sangeet choreography.

200 guests. Everyone said it was the best wedding they'd been to.

So she thought: I should do this for a living.

First client: budget Rs. 5 lakhs. Expectations: Rs. 15 lakhs.

"Can you get us a destination-style mandap? And the food should be like that wedding on Instagram."

She said yes. Because saying no meant losing the client.

She lost Rs. 40,000 on that wedding.

Wedding number four.

The caterer didn't show up.

500 guests. Baraat arriving in 2 hours.

She called every restaurant, every dhaba, every halwai in Amritsar.

Arranged food for 500 in 3 hours.

The client said: "The paneer was cold."

Year one: broke even. Barely.

Year two: two clients defaulted.

One claimed "it wasn't what we discussed."
The other just stopped picking up the phone.

Rs. 2.8 lakhs. Gone.

Peak season is 3 months. The other 9? Silence.

She shut down before year three.

She loved the glamour of weddings.

The lehengas. The decor. The first dance.

The struggle is none of that.

It's vendor management at 3 AM.
Drunk uncles. Families fighting over budgets.
Clients who ghost on payments.

The wedding is one night.
The struggle is the 6 months before it.

Next stop: Bhopal.

A retired army havildar.
A security staffing agency.
And a lesson he learned the hard way:
you're only as good as your worst soldier.

episodes.synopsis: A young woman who started wedding planning after organizing her cousin's wedding. Clients wanted champagne on beer budgets, vendors gave no credit, a caterer no-showed for 500 guests. She broke even year one, lost money year two when clients defaulted. Now works at an established company.
episodes.caption: The wedding is one night. The struggle is the 6 months before it. What's the hardest part of your job that nobody sees?

episodes.title: The Worst Soldier

slides.text: The Worst Soldier

He meets me at his office.

Two rooms above a hardware shop in MP Nagar.

A whiteboard with guard deployment schedules.
A photo of his regiment on the wall.

"In the army, if a soldier fails, the officer is responsible.
Same rule here. Except here, nobody follows rules."

First year: 15 guards deployed across 3 sites.

Corporates wouldn't touch him.
"Small agency. No track record. Come back when you have 100 guards."

So he took whatever he could get.
Residential societies. Small offices. Night shifts nobody wanted.

The poaching started immediately.

A bigger agency offered his guards Rs. 500 more per month.

Three guards left in one week.

"I trained them. Taught them how to stand, how to speak, how to log entries.

They left for a dal-roti difference."

Then it happened.

A guard fell asleep on duty. At his best client's site.

The client's CCTV caught it.
Sent him the footage at 6 AM.

Contract terminated.

Word spread.
"That new agency? Their guards sleep on the job."

One guard. One nap. His reputation was done.

ESIC. PF. Compliance returns.

He'd never filed a form in his life.
The army handled everything.

Now he was drowning in paperwork.
A rival filed a complaint — "untrained guards, no compliance."

He almost quit.

But then he thought about the sleeping guard.
And he got angry. Not at the guard.
At himself.

He started a 2-week training program.

Not just standing at gates.
First aid. Communication. How to handle a crisis.
How to stay awake.

Guards from his agency started looking different.
Talking different. Standing different.

One corporate facility manager noticed.

50-guard contract. Because of the training.

Everyone thinks security staffing is easy.

Hire guards. Deploy guards. Collect payments.

The struggle is finding reliable people.
Training them. Keeping them.
Taking responsibility when they fail.

He chose that struggle because the army taught him one thing:

You're only as good as your worst soldier.

Next stop: Vizag.

A pharmacist who went to war against Apollo and MedPlus.

His weapon? Knowing 200 families by name.

episodes.synopsis: A retired army havildar who started a security guard staffing agency. Guards got poached, one fell asleep on duty costing him a contract, rivals spread rumors. He started a 2-week training program that made his guards visibly different. One corporate gave him a 50-guard contract because of it.
episodes.caption: You're only as good as your worst soldier. What's the weakest link in your work that keeps you up at night?

episodes.title: The Prescription

slides.text: The Prescription

His pharmacy is on a side street in Dwaraka Nagar.

No AC. Ceiling fan. Medicine shelves floor to ceiling.

He's on the phone when I arrive.

"Aunty, your Metformin is due on Thursday. I'll send it."

He knows his customers by their medication.

When he opened his second store, Apollo had zero presence in his area.

Within a year, they opened three.

Discount cards. Loyalty points. Air conditioning.

His customers started walking past his shop to the one with the glass doors.

A supplier dumped near-expiry stock on him.

"Small shop? He won't check."

He caught it. But not before 3 batches went on the shelf.

Had to destroy medicines worth Rs. 45,000.

A pharmacist destroying medicine. That broke something in him.

Then his delivery boy disappeared.

With medicines. With cash.

He spent a week tracking the boy down.

Recovered nothing.

The second store was bleeding money. Eight months in the red.

His wife said: "Close the second shop. One is enough."

He almost did.

Instead, he did something the chains couldn't.

He started calling.

Every chronic patient — diabetes, BP, thyroid.

"Your refill is due. I'll send it home."

No app. No notification.
Just a man who remembered your medicine.

200 families. He knew them all.

11 PM delivery to Mrs. Murthy.
Her husband's insulin ran out.

Apollo was closed.
MedPlus was closed.

He wasn't.

"Beta, you're the only one who picks up at this hour."

That family will never go to Apollo.
Neither will the 15 families she told.

In a war against chains, he won by being personal.

Knowing 200 families' medical histories.
Calling them. Delivering at 11 PM.

That's not a business strategy.

That's a pharmacist who can't stop being a pharmacist.

Next stop: Mysuru.

A couple who thought Instagram followers meant paying clients.

They were wrong.

episodes.synopsis: A pharmacist who opened a second pharmacy when independents were losing to Apollo and MedPlus. Apollo opened 3 stores in his area, suppliers gave near-expiry stock, delivery boy stole medicines. He won by knowing 200 families' prescriptions by heart and calling them to refill.
episodes.caption: The chains keep growing. But there's one thing they can't replicate. When was the last time a business knew you by name?

episodes.title: The Render

slides.text: The Render

They meet me at a cafe in Gokulam.

Both of them. They don't work together anymore.
They barely look at each other.

She orders for herself. He orders for himself.

The business didn't just close.
It left a mark.

They renovated their apartment.
Spent 6 months on it. Did it themselves.

Posted it on Instagram.

2,000 likes. 400 saves. DMs asking: "Who designed this?"

"We did."

"Can you do mine?"

That's how it started. A comment section became a business.

First client: loved the design.
Hated the execution.

The contractor used the wrong shade of paint.
Tiles were uneven.
The modular kitchen arrived — wrong dimensions.

"This doesn't look like the 3D render."

Of course it doesn't. A render isn't real.
But the client paid for real.

Second client changed requirements 11 times.

"Actually, can we do teak instead of plywood?"
"What about an island counter?"
"My mother-in-law wants a pooja room now."

Each change cost money.
They absorbed most of it.

"We didn't know how to say no.
We were new. We were scared they'd leave a bad review."

The carpenter took Rs. 40,000 advance.

Disappeared.

Phone switched off. Workshop locked.

They drove across Mysuru for two weeks looking for him.

Found him working on someone else's kitchen.

With their wood.

4 projects. 14 months. Made money on 1.

The relationship cracked before the business did.

Instagram made it look like a lifestyle.

The struggle is contractor management.
Client hand-holding.
Absorbing cost overruns.

They chose the Instagram dream.

The reality was chasing a carpenter across Mysuru
for Rs. 40,000 and a half-finished kitchen.

The last stop.

Gangtok.

A woman who left Delhi for the mountains.

The same industry that broke someone in Kochi.

A different story.

episodes.synopsis: A couple who started an interior design firm after renovating their home and posting it on Instagram. First client hated execution, second changed requirements 11 times, carpenter disappeared with advance. 4 projects in 14 months. Made money on 1. Relationship strain led to shutdown.
episodes.caption: Instagram followers are not paying clients. What's something that looks easy online but isn't?

episodes.title: The Right Struggle

slides.text: The Right Struggle

The homestay is 40 minutes from Gangtok town.

No signboard on the main road.
A dirt path. Prayer flags.
Kangchenjunga in the distance.

She's making tea when I arrive.
Not chai. A Sikkimese herbal brew.

"You found it. Most guests get lost the first time.
That's part of the charm."

She was in marketing in Delhi.
Good job. Good salary. Corner desk in Gurgaon.

Came to Sikkim on a trip.
Fell in love with the mountains.

Quit 3 months later.

"Everyone thought I was having a breakdown.
Maybe I was. But it was the right kind."

Locals didn't trust her.

"Outsider. Delhi girl. She'll leave in a year."

Permits took 12 months.
Every office had a different requirement.

She rented a room from a local family while she waited.
Learned some Nepali.
Helped at the local school.

Slowly — very slowly — they stopped calling her "the Delhi girl."

First winter: zero guests.

Savings running out.

She took a job at a hotel in Gangtok town.
Housekeeping. Front desk. Whatever they needed.

Worked there 6 months.
Every rupee went into the homestay.

"I cleaned hotel rooms during the day
and built my own place on weekends."

A landslide blocked the road for 2 months.

No guests. No supplies.
She hiked 3 hours to town for groceries.

Budget hotels in town charged Rs. 800/night.
She couldn't compete on price.

"I was losing to places with hot water and WiFi.
I had a view. But you can't eat a view."

Then she stopped trying to be a hotel.

Local food — not menu food. What she ate.
Guided hikes — not tours. Walks she took every morning.
Stories about Sikkim — not a brochure. Her life.

Guests stayed longer. Paid more.
Recommended it to friends.

Not because it was a good hotel.
Because it wasn't a hotel at all.

Remember Episode 9?

Kochi. A houseboat. Tourism.

He saw a YouTube video about houseboat revenue.
Rs. 15,000 per day per boat.
He chased the daily rate.

Same industry. Same struggles.
Seasonality. Weather. Isolation.

He wanted the money.
She wanted the mountains.

He sold the boat in 18 months.
She's been here 6 years.

She didn't build a business.
She built a life she wanted to live.
And charged people to share it.

The Kochi houseboat guy wanted Rs. 15,000/day.
She wanted to wake up in the mountains.

That's why she survived the same struggles
that broke him.

That's 25 cities. 25 stories.

Some made it. Some didn't.

The difference was never the business plan.
It was whether they chose the right struggle.

If you're thinking of starting something —
don't ask "how much will I make?"

Ask "what am I willing to endure?"

Thank you for travelling with me.

Share Episode 1 with someone who's thinking of starting something.

Follow @the.unwritten.rules.

episodes.synopsis: A woman who left a Delhi marketing job for an eco-homestay in Gangtok. Locals were skeptical, permits took a year, first winter nobody came. She stopped trying to be a hotel and made it an experience. Same industry as Episode 9's Kochi houseboat failure — but she chose the struggle, not the outcome.
episodes.caption: 25 cities. 25 stories. One question: what struggle would you choose? Thank you for being here.
